articles.title: Why Mamdani opposes RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's NYC event
articles.content: Zohran Mamdani called the Hindu nationalist group's ideology "exclusionary" ahead of Mohan Bhagwat's New York event. But can the mayor do anything to stop it? New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he does not support an upcoming event featuring Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Hindu nationalist group Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), though he acknowledged the city likely has no power to stop it. Bhagwat is scheduled to speak Saturday at Madison Square Garden as part of what organizers are calling the "Universal Oneness Celebration," an event expected to draw around 5,000 attendees, local media reported. It is part of a broader global outreach tour tied to the RSS's centenary year, wherein Bhagwat is visiting the United States, Canada and the UK. When asked whether the event should be canceled at a press conference, Mamdani said: "I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on canceling a private event." Mamdani is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor in New York City's history. He added that his opposition to the visit reflected his role leading a city that believes in "the belonging of each and every person, no matter their color, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from." His mother is acclaimed Indian filmmaker Mira Nair. He added that he grew up with an understanding of India as "a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India." "It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision." The event is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, which says it has backing from over 135 Hindu American organizations and is meant to promote shared heritage and interfaith unity. However, several interfaith and civil rights groups – including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York – have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history. They held a news conference outside New York City Hall calling for the event to be canceled. "Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus. He leads an extremist Hindu nationalist movement that has fueled violence, exclusion and fear for minority communities," said Sravya Tadepalli, Deputy Executive Director of Hindus for Human Rights, in a statement. "New York should not provide the RSS with a stage on which religious nationalism can be repackaged as unity." The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS, is a right-wing Hindu organization founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in 1925. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for National Volunteer Organization. The group describes itself as a "Hindu-centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus and disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance. The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization. In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities. The US government advisory body called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims." United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more. India's BJP-led government denies any discriminatory intent, pointing to programs such as food subsidies and electrification initiatives, which it says benefit all communities. The organization has been banned in India on multiple occasions, including in 1948 after a Hindu nationalist who had ties with the RSS assassinated independence leader Mahatma Gandhi. Abdul El-Sayed catches Trump’s attention with pitch for ‘Trumpcare’
articles.content: President Donald Trump responded on Saturday to Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s push for universal healthcare after the progressive Michigan Democrat pitched that it be called “Trumpcare.” “Donald, this is on the table,” El-Sayed wrote in a post on X last week. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.” El-Sayed, a former public health official who made Medicare for All a cornerstone of his campaign, included mock images of “Trumpcare” cards in the post. The cards are branded with the title named after the president and are golden, an homage to Trump’s favorite color. Trump reposted a screenshot of El-Sayed’s post on Truth Social Saturday, though he didn’t include any text with it. However, he said in a phone interview with Fox News earlier in the day that he believes the government could “do tremendous things on healthcare” after Democrats take control of Congress in January. “They have some good points on healthcare, and they have some bad points, and we have some good things, and probably they would say we have some bad things,” Trump said, referring to congressional Democrats. “But there’s a chance we could get great healthcare and a lot of other things, and we do it in a bipartisan way.” Trump also told reporters at a press conference Friday that he is “open to great healthcare.” “There’s a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare,” he said. “It can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans.” Despite touting his openness to work with Democrats, Trump has also repeatedly emphasized his power to veto legislation since Republican losses in the midterms. “I’ll get along, probably, with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive,” Trump said the day after the election. “But I have the power of the veto.” Trump did say in the interview with Fox News on Saturday that he does not think that vetoing “everything” passed by Democrats for the next two years is the way to go. But he also posted another image of himself on Truth Social later in the day, showing him in a red “VETO”-branded hat and a matching jacket. In a statement Saturday afternoon, El-Sayed said he is “happy to chat” with the president if his intentions to work together on healthcare are genuine. “If the President is serious about meeting the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country, I’m ready to work alongside leaders in the Senate like Senators Van Hollen, Sanders, Wyden, and Warren to deliver,” El-Sayed said. “President Trump, give me a call.”

Democrats who swept into the Senate promised change. A leadership vote is testing them early
articles.description: Democrats who swept into the Senate promised change. A leadership vote is testing them early AP News Van Hollen, once an insider, has started Democrats’ first big fight The Washington Post Alsobrooks-Van Hollen fallout, county executives scramble, freshmen postings, in political notes Maryland Matters Race to lead Senate Democrats the latest battlefield in party’s tussle over Israel The Guardian Here Are the Senators
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Democratic Party’s incoming senators haven’t even been sworn into office yet, but the decision over who will lead their new majority is already testing the promise of change they made as candidates. The 13 new Democrats are part of the largest incoming Senate class in decades, with several winning in Republican strongholds by promising to shake up Washington and be independent voices. Now they are caught up in a classic insider fight, forced to decide whether to stick with longtime Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York or back challenger Chris Van Hollen of Maryland. Newly elected progressives, including Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, have backed Van Hollen, who is taking on Schumer with promises of a more aggressive legislative approach. Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio, who is returning to Washington after losing his seat in 2024, supports Schumer. But the incoming senators from traditionally Republican states such as Texas, Mississippi, Iowa and South Carolina, whose victories helped deliver Democrats the majority, have so far largely avoided taking sides publicly. Annie Andrews of South Carolina has said she is talking with both candidates. Scott Colom of Mississippi says he wants to get to know them better before deciding and describes himself as being in “listening mode.” Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said Thursday he would not back Schumer, but declined to endorse anyone. “I’m looking for someone who is going to bring people together,” Hamilton told MSNow. “Right now, in places like Kansas, there’s a lot of people who don’t feel that in Chuck Schumer.” Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton speaks to supporters during an election night event, Nov. 3, 2026, in Overland Park, Kan. (AP Photo/Charlie Riedel, File) Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton speaks to supporters during an election night event, Nov. 3, 2026, in Overland Park, Kan. (AP Photo/Charlie Riedel, File) Schumer’s long-standing relationships and knowledge of Senate machinery are a big advantage heading into the Dec. 1 vote, which will be held by secret ballot. He also oversees Senate Democrats’ campaign spending group, funneling millions into many of the races and, in some cases, recruiting the candidates to run in the first place. But the reluctance of many incoming senators to commit has put an unusual spotlight on first-term lawmakers who could help shape the party’s direction in the new Congress. “We should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here,” said Hawaii Sen. Mazie Hirono, who is supporting Schumer. “We have to make sure that all these voices are heard, and they’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table.” Many of the incoming senators campaigned as political outsiders, promising to bring fresh perspectives to a Washington establishment they argued had failed ordinary Americans. Andrews, a 46-year-old pediatrician, became the first Democrat in nearly three decades to win a Senate race in South Carolina. She called for “generational change” and said that she would not support Schumer. But she has also rejected policies that Van Hollen supports, such as “Medicare for All.” On a press call Tuesday, Andrews said she has made “no decision” on the majority leader’s race. “The way I assess the situation as it is right now is that the generational change is represented by this incredibly dynamic incoming freshman class of senators,” Andrews said. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico called for “new blood” in the Democratic Party, arguing that fresh perspectives were needed to change a political system that had failed. But Talarico has stopped short of rejecting Schumer, saying in a CBS interview two days after the Nov. 3 election that he would meet with the leadership candidates and ask “tough questions.” From left, Sen.-elect Annie Andrews, D-S.C., Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas, and Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, D-Maine, walk together as newly-elected senators arrive for orientation following a sweeping victory by Democrats in the midterm elections, at the Capitol in Washington, Nov. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite, File) From left, Sen.-elect Annie Andrews, D-S.C., Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas, and Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, D-Maine, walk together as newly-elected senators arrive for orientation following a sweeping victory by Democrats in the midterm elections, at the Capitol in Washington, Nov. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite, File) Iowa Sen.-elect Josh Turek has taken a similar approach, saying his decision will depend on which candidate best reflects the priorities he campaigned on. During a news conference Monday, he said that he had met with Schumer and Van Hollen and was waiting for “further updates” on questions he had. “Whoever provides those answers to me that most closely align with my common sense, prairie populist agenda that I’ve been running on for the last year and a half, that’s who I’ll support,” Turek said. Alaska Sen.-elect Mary Peltola, whose race was officially called on Wednesday, told The Associated Press soon after that she had not yet thought about the leadership race. El-Sayed and Flanagan have been among the staunch supporters of Van Hollen. Another progressive, Maine Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, has said he wouldn’t support Schumer but hasn’t yet said he would vote for Van Hollen. Schumer backed alternative candidates during the primaries in all three races. He supported all three once they were nominated. Senate leadership elections have traditionally been private affairs, decided by lawmakers in closed-door, secret-ballot votes that are shaped by the complicated inner workings of the Senate. The job requires holding together a caucus with competing political interests, a responsibility that doesn’t always align with the demands of the party’s most vocal activists. Schumer’s allies point to his success in doing that job, most recently in the midterms. He helped recruit candidates such as Brown, Peltola and North Carolina Sen.-elect Roy Cooper, while his allied super PAC was the largest Democratic spender in tightly contested races such as in Michigan and Maine. “When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract,” Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego said. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., center, poses for a photograph in his office with Sen.-elects Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, James Talarico, D-Texas, Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., Josh Turek, D-Iowa, Roy Cooper, D-N.C., Juliana Stratton, D-Ill., Chris Pappas, D-N.H., Annie Andrews, D-S.C., Troy Jackson, D-Maine, Peggy Flanagan, D-Minn., and Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, at the U.S. Capitol in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., center, poses for a photograph in his office with Sen.-elects Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, James Talarico, D-Texas, Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., Josh Turek, D-Iowa, Roy Cooper, D-N.C., Juliana Stratton, D-Ill., Chris Pappas, D-N.H., Annie Andrews, D-S.C., Troy Jackson, D-Maine, Peggy Flanagan, D-Minn., and Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, at the U.S. Capitol in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) But Democrats are also facing pressure from some in their base to confront Republican President Donald Trump more aggressively while delivering on ambitious policy promises. Large progressive organizations, including MoveOn and Indivisible, have endorsed Van Hollen, while many senators’ offices have been flooded with calls urging them to reject Schumer. “Our members are tired of politicians content with incrementalism — they want bold, creative leadership that will help Democrats usher in affordability and accountability without delay or compromise in the next Congress,” MoveOn’s executive director, Joel Payne, said in a statement. At a Schumer news conference Wednesday, several activists shouted from a distance, “Step down, Schumer! Step down, Schumer!” The fifth-term senator has not said whether his term ending in 2028 will be his last. Van Hollen, a supporter of progressive priorities including Medicare for All and restrictions on offensive weapons transfers to Israel, has promised a more confrontational approach to Trump, an ambitious economic agenda and changes to how the party operates in primaries. The leadership fight has also drawn in more established Democrats, including senators whose political ambitions may include higher office. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, fresh off a reelection victory in a presidential battleground state, is among the Democrats whose names have surfaced as potential White House contenders in 2028. Ossoff has served under Schumer’s leadership for nearly six years. “I haven’t committed to any candidate, and I’ll hear everybody out,” Ossoff said this week. Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, elected in 2024 and now contemplating a presidential bid, said Thursday she was supporting Van Hollen. A moderate who has called for change in Senate leadership, Slotkin has also been critical of some of Van Hollen’s more progressive policies, underscoring how the leadership fight cuts across the party’s ideological divisions. “Because I’ve been clear that I wasn’t supporting Schumer, I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen,” Slotkin said. Associated Press writers Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, Meg Kinnard in Columbia, S.C., and Steven Sloan and Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report.

articles.description: Director Takashi Yamazaki ups the ante by pitting Godzilla against one of the monster's greatest foes
articles.content: It's a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki's sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most. (Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We'll give you a heads-up when we get there.) As I wrote previously, Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One, setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945.Read full article Comments

articles.description: Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.
articles.content: Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI. Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.” “Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.” Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS. articles.title: Taiwan warns Canada’s Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks
articles.content: HALIFAX, Nova Scotia (AP) — Taiwan’s deputy foreign minister warned on Saturday that Prime Minister Mark Carney risks exposing Canada to the very economic coercion he has cautioned against by deepening trade ties with China, saying that Taiwan has learned the hard way that dependence on Beijing comes with consequences. “We worry. We worry,” Chen Ming-chi told The Associated Press in an interview at the Halifax International Security Forum when asked about Carney’s efforts to improve relations with China. Carney has warned that major powers are using economic integration as a weapon, citing U.S. tariffs and China’s restrictions on critical minerals. He has urged middle powers to diversify their trade relationships to avoid economic coercion. Chen praised Carney’s speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, but questioned whether Canada should deepen ties with countries that don’t share its democratic values. “Who do you want to choose as your partners?” he asked. “You have your own history. You have two Michaels,” Chen said, referring to former Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig and businessman Michael Spavor, whose ne arly three-year detention in China prompted accusations of hostage diplomacy. The two were arrested in 2018 shortly after Canada detained Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou on a U.S. extradition request. They were released in September 2021, the same day Meng returned to China. Beijing denied their detention was politically motivated. Chen’s warning came days after Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and agreed to additional tariff reductions as Canada seeks to diversify trade during U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war. Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if negotiations with Washington fail to preserve a viable Canadian auto industry. Trump has threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts beginning on Jan. 1. Chen warned that Chinese electric vehicles could threaten Canadian manufacturers and pose surveillance risks because of their connected technology, even if manufactured in Canada. Carney has argued that Canada’s trade relationship with China differs from Washington’s more complicated ties with Beijing. Canada primarily exports agricultural products, energy and other commodities rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors. Chen said that Taiwan had dramatically reduced its economic dependence on China after experiencing Beijing’s use of trade restrictions to exert political pressure. “They are very good at weaponizing interdependence,” he said. “They are very good at leveraging our dependence to reach political goals.” Taiwan reduced the share of its outbound investment going to China from more than 80% in 2010 to 3.8% last year, Chen said. Its exports to China and Hong Kong fell from nearly 44% of total exports in 2020 to about 27% last year, according to Taiwanese government figures. Chen also accused Beijing of exploiting a striking photograph from this week’s summit in Shenzhen showing Xi seated prominently between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to project China as the world’s leading power. “The main idea is to prove not only to his domestic audience that he is the world leader,” Chen said. “They are so good at propaganda.” He described the summit as “more symbolic than substantial.” Chen said China was intensifying military operations around Taiwan, despite the potentially enormous costs of an invasion. He warned that Chinese vessels could be rehearsing for a maritime quarantine of the self-governing island. Despite his concerns about Beijing, Chen praised Carney’s international leadership and welcomed his commitment to sign a long-delayed trade cooperation arrangement with Taiwan. “We have a high respect of Prime Minister Carney’s vision. And we want to be part of this vision,” he said.

articles.description: Iran strikes 3 tankers as it shows off missile launchers, and other Mideast news AP News Iran unveils dual-missile launcher, new ‘missile city’: What to know Al Jazeera IRGC Chief Visits Missile City تسنیم How war shifted Iran's missile ambitions beyond the Middle East Al-Monitor Iran posts video of new underground ‘missile city’ NewsNation
articles.content: Iran unveiled a new missile launcher at an underground facility, touting what it says is its continued capability to strike if the war with the United States and Israel accelerates once more. Meanwhile, in the Gaza Strip, an Israeli airstrike hit a truck carrying food, killing three men, the head of Shifa Hospital said. The Israeli military said that it struck Islamic Jihad militants. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here. Iranian state television aired footage from an underground missile facility where the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard unveiled a new launcher that it said was capable of firing two liquid-fueled missiles. The launchers appear to be an advance over a dual launcher that Iran previously used that fired two solid-fuel missiles at a time. Liquid fuel is more efficient and gives operators some capability to adjust the missiles’ speed and trajectory. The location of the missile site wasn’t revealed, but the broadcast aimed to tout Iran’s missile capabilities and counter statements from Washington that the U.S. has destroyed the missile program. During the unveiling of the launchers, Brig. Gen. Seyyed Majid Mousavi, commander of the Guard’s Aerospace Force, said that Iran’s “capabilities have expanded significantly.” Separately, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Saturday that Tehran remained in contact with mediators from Qatar who visited Iran on Friday to explore “whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy.” At least three oil tankers were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday in what appeared to be the latest Iranian strikes on shipping through the strategic chokepoint. The U.K. military’s maritime security center said two tankers were struck separately by projectiles early Saturday while exiting the Persian Gulf through the strait. There were no reports of casualties, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center reported. There was no immediate comment from Iran on the center’s report. The Iranian navy said in a statement carried on state media that a tanker hit a naval mine east of the strait and caught fire. State media also said that the military carried out its most “intense and varied” operations yet in the strait overnight to stop vessels. Iranian forces have been attacking shipping through the strait in a campaign aimed at hiking global energy prices to pressure the United States, which has imposed a crippling blockade on Iranian ports. An Israeli strike hit a truck carrying food in Gaza City’s Tel al-Hawa district on Saturday, killing three men, Mohamed Abu Selmiya, the director of Shifa Hospital, told The Associated Press. Videos circulating online showed a pickup truck reduced to twisted metal with boxes of cooked rice torn open in the back. It wasn’t immediately known where the food was being taken or whether it was connected to an aid organization. Most of Gaza’s more than 2 million people are homeless and dependent on food distributions by the United Nations and other aid groups. The Israeli military said later Saturday that it had struck Islamic Jihad militants who were traveling in a vehicle used to transport food and logistical supplies to fellow militants. The vehicle wasn’t visibly marked as belonging to a humanitarian aid organization, the military said. One of the men had been fired from such an organization after Israel’s military notified it of his militant role, a military official said on condition of anonymity in line with military regulations. The men were targeted because they had “advanced attacks” against Israel’s military and civilians in recent weeks, the military added. Since a ceasefire deal with Hamas came into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes have killed more than 1,650 people, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn’t distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll, but says women and children make up around half the dead. In a Saturday address to mark Lebanon’s independence day, President Joseph Aoun said that the country faced two “fundamental obstacles”: Israel’s occupation and “foreign interference in our affairs — specifically by certain influential elements within the Iranian regime.” Aoun said that Israel should withdraw from Lebanon, but defended the two countries’ first direct talks in decades, saying “diplomacy is not surrender.” He said: “The era of weapons outside state control has come to an end” — a reference to Iran-backed Hezbollah militants, who began firing on Israel right after the start of the Iran war. The group has refused to hand over its weapons while Israel is occupying parts of southern Lebanon. Sally Abou AlJoud reported from Beirut, and Wafaa Shurafa from Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip.

articles.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
articles.description: We created a list of the most notable AI agents that can live in your text messages, from general assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
articles.content: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.” The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees. Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished. Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps. It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally. Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background. Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant. According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes, “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.” Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car. Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion, valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security.) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls. Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request. Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app. It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention. It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages. It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action. The platform also offers hundreds of integrations, including Discord, Gmail, and Slack, allowing it to connect with the apps you already use. It’s currently in beta and free to use on iMessage. There’s also a Pro version for €27 per month (or approximately $30.25 USD), which includes 500 tasks a month, 20 connected apps, scheduled tasks, and memory. Miso takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel. It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. Users can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details and flight updates, along with personalized recommendations. Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life. Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family. It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month. Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household. It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services. Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household. Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital. Users can interact with Pally as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of plans, receipts, dates, files, and other details. There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram. Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures. Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later. Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images. Rene is currently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp. Instead of waiting for users to open an app, Skye is an “agentic homescreen” for the iPhone that analyzes information from connected services and surfaces what it thinks is relevant through contextual cards, suggestions, and daily briefings. The assistant can generate audio briefings, prepare information ahead of meetings, surface reminders, and identify potentially useful information. The company, Signull Labs, raised about $3.6 million in seed funding in 2025. It entered private testing and beta in April 2026, and hasn’t yet announced a public release date. articles.content: Lionsgate's latest title notched the third-best opening Friday in the six-movie dystopian series, representing a major revival after 2023's 'The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.' The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping has begun to ignite the box office. Lionsgate released the sixth film in the dystopian franchise in 4,018 North American theaters, and it grossed $56 million on Friday, including Thursday previews, as it heads for more than $120 million for the weekend. This would give it the third-best debut Friday in franchise history, besting the two Mockingjay titles ($55.1 million for 2014’s Part 1, $45.6 million for 2015’s Part 2) and 2023’s The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes ($19 million) but behind 2013’s Catching Fire ($70.9 million) and 2012’s The Hunger Games ($67.2 million). Sunrise earned an A- CinemaScore from audiences, putting it below the A grades of the Jennifer Lawrence-led initial 2012 movie that kicked off the series and 2013’s Catching Fire but matching the A- grades of the two Mockingjay films. Related Stories Movies How 'I Play Rocky' Star P.J. Byrne Became One of Hollywood's Go-To Character Actors Beyond the Book "The Secrecy Was Insane:" The Making of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,' From Locked Safes to Original Cast's Return The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will notch the fifth-biggest opening in Lionsgate history, as it also stands at No. 5 among 2026 domestic openings for all studios. It represents the highest-grossing launch for the careers of stars Glenn Close, Jesse Plemons, Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning. This weekend’s haul also brings the Hunger Games franchise’s box office total to roughly $3.437 billion to make it the studio’s highest-grossing franchise ever, topping The Twilight Saga. Lionsgate had projected The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping to gross north of $80 million, but other sources expected that it would collect between $100 million and $130 million, which now looks to be the case. Adapting author Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel that was published last year, director Francis Lawrence‘s movie carries a production budget of roughly $150 million as it revitalizes the franchise in telling a story set 24 years before the events of Collins’ original 2008 book. This opening represents a major comeback for the series after registering its lowest-performing entry with 2023 prequel The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, given that Sunrise on the Reaping is looking to open with more than double its launch. Starring Tom Blyth, Rachel Zegler and Hunter Schafer, Songbirds & Snakes — telling the backstory for the villainous President Snow, played by Ralph Fiennes in the new movie — disappointed, opening to $44 million domestically for the weekend before ending its run with $166.4 million domestically and a global sum of $361.8 million. It earned a B+ CinemaScore, the lowest for the franchise. Sunrise on the Reaping holds a 67 percent critical score on Rotten Tomatoes, lagging behind the franchise’s first four movies but besting the 64 percent approval for Songbirds & Snakes. The new film has a franchise-best 95 audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter, chief film critic David Rooney wrote that it “delivers on emotion and brutal spectacle.” The movie opened the day after the launch of the hotly anticipated video game Grand Theft Auto 6, which does not appear to be preventing the film from thriving. Joseph Zada stars as Haymitch Abernathy, providing the backstory for the character whom Woody Harrelson brought to life in the first four movies. The cast for Sunrise on the Reaping also includes Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak and Maya Hawke. Among other weekend titles, Amazon MGM Studios expanded I Play Rocky to 2,477 North American locations after two frames in limited release. Peter Farrelly’s Rocky origin story earned $3.8 million on Friday, including Thursday previews, as it heads for an estimated $9.3 million. Starring Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone, I Play Rocky landed a rare A+ CinemaScore, becoming only the second release this year to do so (after April’s A Great Awakening). I Play Rocky holds an 89 percent approval rating from critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 98 percent audience score. Rooney’s review described it as a “big-hearted movie about moviemaking, if not an artful one.” In its sophomore frame, Paramount’s horror-tinged holiday offering Ebenezer is likely to claim third place with roughly $8.2 million for a decline of around 57 percent, bringing its domestic cume to $33 million. Johnny Depp marks his studio comeback vehicle with director Ti West’s reimagining of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol, which opened atop last weekend’s box office. Continuing to draw families in its third weekend is Warner Bros.’ The Cat in the Hat, as the animated adaptation of Dr. Seuss’ classic children’s book is expected to gross around $7 million for a domestic total of $47.2 million. This marks a respectable decline of roughly 38 percent for directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni’s movie that features the voice of Bill Hader in the lead role. It is set to face fresh competition in the animated space from Disney’s Hexed over the forthcoming Thanksgiving frame. Gkids and Toho’s Godzilla Minus Zero is likely to close out the top five with $2.9 million in its third weekend to reach a domestic cume of around $54.7 million. Focus Features opened Elsinore in six theaters in New York and Los Angeles, with director Simon Stone’s Oscar hopeful likely to collect approximately $240,000 to average $40,000 per screen. Andrew Scott stars in the biographical film about Scottish actor Ian Charleson, who navigates personal challenges while preparing for a pivotal performance of Hamlet. After earning acclaim at Telluride and TIFF, Elsinore holds an 87 percent rating from critics on Rotten Tomatoes, with Rooney deeming it “a hymn to the theater, powered by a towering lead turn.” Toward the bottom of the top 10 is Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, with Sony Pictures distributing the Prime Focus Studios religious epic that is expected to gross $2 million for its third weekend to bring its domestic take to $28.3 million through Sunday. Director Nitesh Tiwari’s project becomes the highest-grossing Indian film ever at the North American box office. With Thanksgiving arriving next weekend, the holiday frame brings an array of new options, including Disney’s Hexed, Universal’s Meet the Parents sequel Focker-in-Law, Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth and Angel’s biographical Hershey. The supposed warning signs? A nationwide […]
articles.content: Cases of bottled water are displayed for sale at a Costco in Burbank, Calif. Doomsday conspiracy theories circulating online have fueled calls for Americans to stockpile food, water and emergency supplies amid unfounded predictions of widespread blackouts and other catastrophes. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Stock up on food and medicine. Fill containers with water. Prepare to live off the grid for at least 90 days. Those were among the warnings circulating on social media in recent weeks, as online posts predicted a looming national catastrophe and urged Americans to prepare for the worst. The supposed warning signs? A nationwide flight shutdown, disruptions to banking and technology services and a routine federal emergency alert test — seemingly unrelated events that some online users portrayed as evidence of a coordinated cyberattack or impending emergency. The doomsday predictions lack credible evidence. But the speculation comes as the nation’s aging infrastructure faces mounting vulnerabilities from extreme weather, rising energy demands and cyberthreats — raising legitimate questions about the country’s preparedness for major disruptions. Federal officials have said they found no evidence that the latest disruptions were connected or that a nationwide emergency was imminent. And some emergency management experts warn that false alarms can undermine public trust in official warnings and complicate disaster response when real emergencies strike. Still, the attention surrounding these unfounded predictions does not necessarily mean they have gained widespread acceptance. Joseph Uscinski, a political science professor at the University of Miami who studies conspiracy theories, cautioned against interpreting viral posts as evidence of a broader shift in public beliefs. “Your average conspiracy theory dies on the vine,” he said, noting that many fade as the news cycle moves on. Uscinski described the reaction as a recurring pattern: A major event sparks conspiracy theories, those claims attract attention and then eventually fade, only for the cycle to repeat when another event captures the public’s attention. Some of the latest rumors appeared to gain traction ahead of Tuesday’s nationwide Emergency Alert System test, which interrupted television and radio broadcasts across the country. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, or FEMA, and the Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, had announced the Nov. 17 test in September as part of routine efforts to evaluate the nation’s emergency warning infrastructure. Federal rules require nationwide testing at least once every three years. The timing of the test, combined with recent outages and national security concerns, fueled speculation that the government was preparing Americans for a major catastrophe. FEMA addressed the claims on Facebook, saying the test was scheduled in advance and unrelated to any impending disaster. “We love a good fan theory as much as anyone, but there is no secret emergency happening here,” the agency’s post read. From technical glitches to doomsday warnings The online speculation followed several high-profile disruptions this month, including a major Microsoft service outage Nov. 12-14, and a nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration on Nov. 13. Microsoft attributed its disruptions to technical problems. And the FAA blamed work by a contractor upgrading a router in Arkansas. But this week brought more disruptions: to several major banks Monday, to Apple services and the National Security Agency’s internal network Tuesday. Those also were separate technical issues, officials said. Adding to the national security concerns, CNN reported Monday that U.S. intelligence suggested Iran was developing plans to potentially target senior Trump administration officials with a radioactive “dirty bomb” or chemical weapon in Washington, D.C. US Senate panel grills Trump cyber director about outages making people ‘jittery’ U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that he did not believe there was an imminent threat to Washington. Iran also denied the allegations. During a congressional hearing Wednesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told lawmakers that threats from Iran against Americans at home and abroad had increased substantially. Asked specifically about the reported dirty-bomb plot, Clayton declined to discuss the intelligence but acknowledged that threats involving weapons capable of causing mass casualties were not new. Despite those explanations, social media posts increasingly portrayed the events as connected. Some TikTok videos warned of a 90-day nationwide blackout that was to begin Nov. 17, while other videos encouraged viewers to stockpile emergency supplies, including water, food and medicine. One widely circulated video manipulated footage of President Donald Trump speaking at a Nov. 9 news conference to make it appear that he had announced an impending blackout, according to a PolitiFact investigation. Trump made no such announcement. The account sharing the manipulated footage also promoted cryptocurrency purchases ahead of the supposed national emergency. Other online posts pointed to a federal Department of Defense initiative announced in September to help military installations operate independently of civilian power grids for at least 90 days. The initiative, known as FORTRESS America, is intended to strengthen military readiness during potential disruptions. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also dismissed the online warnings, telling Fox News that Americans did not need to stockpile supplies in anticipation of widespread disruptions to electricity or to food and water sources. Vice President JD Vance similarly sought to ease concerns Monday, saying Americans did not need to build bunkers or rush to stockpile food and water in response to the recent outages. “We do not see some crisis coming down, but you have to be prepared for everything,” Vance said during an interview with Fox News. Other countries, including the United Kingdom, France and Germany, have urged residents to prepare for severe weather, cyberattacks and other emergencies –– adding to confusion among some Americans about whether they should take similar precautions. The UK launched its “Be Ready” campaign in October suggesting a three-day supply in case of emergency. Real vulnerabilities The conspiracy theories have emerged against a backdrop of genuine concerns about the nation’s aging infrastructure and growing cybersecurity threats, which have exposed vulnerabilities in systems Americans rely on for electricity, transportation, healthcare and emergency services. The American Society of Civil Engineers gave U.S. infrastructure an overall C grade in its 2025 report card, a slight improvement from the C- awarded in 2021. The national report card is released every four years. FEMA chief, US House members push for emergency management changes But the organization warned that significant vulnerabilities remain. The nation’s energy and aviation infrastructure each received a D+, and the report estimated a $3.7 trillion gap between planned infrastructure investments and what is needed to bring the country’s systems into good working order. The recent disruptions also drew scrutiny on Capitol Hill on Thursday, where lawmakers questioned Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, about the nation’s ability to withstand cyberthreats. “American citizens are jittery,” Michigan Democratic U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin said during the Senate Homeland Security Committee hearing, raising concerns about the Trump administration’s elimination of more than 1,000 positions at the agency. The nominee, Michael LoSapio, declined to assess the agency’s current resources but said he would evaluate potential gaps and request additional funding if necessary. Cyberattacks are a growing concern for critical infrastructure operators, as hackers target hospitals, utilities, government agencies and other essential services. “Modern society is effectively built on interdependence and high levels of complexity of technologies supporting human systems, and so when you get kind of a localized failure, it can very quickly cascade to more strategic problems,” said Charles Harry, an associate research professor at the University of Maryland who specializes in cybersecurity risk and previously worked for the National Security Agency. Harry pointed to healthcare and transportation as examples of sectors where interconnected systems can allow disruptions to spread far beyond their original source. Hundreds of thousands of cyberattacks occur every day, but most attract little public attention because they cause minimal disruption, Harry said. The landscape is evolving as artificial intelligence gives cybercriminals, state-sponsored hackers and even less sophisticated attackers new tools, putting additional pressure on organizations to address security weaknesses before they can be exploited. “Over the last 12 months, we’ve seen just an explosion in this type of activity, and it means that we’re going to have more frequent attacks, more consequential attacks,” Harry said. When misinformation becomes a public safety threat Beyond the latest doomsday predictions, the spread of false information presents a broader challenge for state and local emergency management agencies, which rely on public trust to communicate accurate information during disasters. FEMA chief decries rumors, disinformation about hurricane recovery as worst ever During an actual emergency, false or misleading information can divert critical resources, delay response efforts and create confusion about evacuation routes, available shelters and government assistance. “Sometimes (misinformation) can even mask itself as being something that comes from us, so you really have to dig deep, look at where the messages are coming from,” said Marc Pappas, the president of the National Emergency Management Association and director of the Rhode Island Emergency Management Agency. The consequences have already played out during real emergencies. Following Hurricanes Helene and Milton in 2024, conspiracy theories shared online alleged that the federal government had deliberately created or steered the storms toward certain communities. Other false claims accused federal officials of withholding disaster assistance, confiscating property and preventing private organizations from delivering supplies. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, publicly debunked the weather manipulation claims, emphasizing that no technology exists to create or steer hurricanes. FEMA also launched an online “rumor response” page to counter misinformation and reassure survivors that assistance remained available. The challenges facing emergency officials come as the Trump administration considers shifting more disaster response responsibilities to state and local governments. During a U.S. House hearing Thursday, FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton called for significant changes to the agency, arguing that stronger states would make the nation more prepared and resilient. Some lawmakers questioned whether states have the resources to take on additional responsibilities. “Emergency management is ready. We continue to be ready and prepared for emergencies, threats that happen to occur across the nation,” Pappas told Stateline, arguing that state agencies are well equipped to take on additional disaster response responsibilities. articles.title: Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd
articles.description: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, Alaska's governor-elect, has made more than 13,000 WIkipedia edits.
articles.content: We have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office. That means there’s a lot more snooping into politicians’ online pasts to come. This month’s elections were no exception. Earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska, making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959. But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor. On a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011. The governor-elect is also from Alaska, went to Yale, and climbs mountains. Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most important sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate. This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator. Check this guy out! A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia! But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his. “The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero. Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied. Fair enough. If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them. But I’m a journalist. I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong. If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped. So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more important messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account. So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.content: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years. All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets. You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure, something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder. Thanks. Great to be here. I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos. I know. It’s like a normal thing that happened. It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash. [Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people. Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem. Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!” What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it? I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later. But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell. I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good. So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this. --- [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/24792604/The_Verge_Decoder_Tileart.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better. Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first? Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now. Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that. Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year. I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs. Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work? They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw one estimate from Steve Rattner saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry. But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today. I was chatting with a bunch of corporate governance experts and law professors and they were all saying Anthropic, like OpenAI, has such an unusual corporate structure that they aren’t actually beholden to shareholders in the way that some public companies are. Shareholders can never vote out executives. They don’t have a lot of power to influence anything really. It’s the founders and this special trust, which we can get to in a second, that have the power. But either way, they were all saying it doesn’t matter if shareholders have a say here really in voting. It’s about the fact that no matter who has a say, Anthropic is going to be under so much pressure to make money and to buy compute and catch up with OpenAI in that way, that this is going to be a huge reckoning for them. We’re probably going to see a lot of things fall by the wayside, maybe even some expensive safety efforts. I want to come to the governance structure angle here. We live in a time of Nvidia scandals. Corporate governance is all the rage now. It’s the hottest topic in American business, but let’s come to that in one minute. I just want to stay on “can you sell a token for a dollar more than it cost you to make it” for one more turn. It’s just the dumbest way of thinking about this. Anthropic rents capacity from big cloud providers, from hyperscalers. They run the GPUs in them. They pay for power, they pay for the GPUs. There’s some input cost and then they have to sell the token for more than all those input costs. That is the dumbest way of thinking about their business. I promise you that they think about it in a more sophisticated way than that, but that is how I think about it. I was just at the Microsoft Ignite conference this week and I saw Satya Nadella and he was very clear to me and others that they’re going to try to bring the price of tokens down, that their whole system is designed to make all the AI vendors fungible underneath Copilot and they’ll pick the best model for the task and make sure you get the cheapest one for whatever it is you’re trying to do. That seems totally at odds with what Anthropic needs to do, which is get more and more margin for every single token they sell so they can keep renting capacity from data centers or buy more chips than OpenAI or whatever it is they need to do. How are they structured to solve that problem? Is it just more people using AI or is it more expensive tokens? I think it’s a little of both, and it’s interesting because Anthropic has been kind of sneakily trying to do this. We wrote a piece in the past year about how there was a big outcry, particularly focused on Anthropic, for passing on costs to consumers. Individuals who were customers of Anthropic were really mad because they felt like the prices were going up for the same stuff or for worse quality and that costs were just getting passed on to them. This became a thing across the industry, a big outcry, but Anthropic bore the brunt of it. Anthropic had to have a public statement. They’re like, “Look, we’re going to work on this.” And they did roll it back a little, but I mean, they’ve got to keep doing it in some way. The other thing they’re focused on is hoping that their models are going to be good enough that people just form an attachment — not emotionally, well maybe — but form an attachment to them and they can moat people in. They’re all about the moat these days: “We’ve got to build a moat.” OpenAI is about this, too. They want so much of your everyday life and business to be married to Anthropic’s tools that it’d be really hard to port it all over and you won’t want to and you’ll just keep paying. So that’s what they’re going for. They’re also, of course, hoping that enterprise and government contracts are going to really make up a bunch of this, in which case you don’t have to worry quite as much about nickel-and-diming because they’ve got a lot of money. But I think that’s the interesting part here. When it comes to people that do care about the price a lot, they’re just trying to moat them in and hope for the best.
