After the Blue Wave, climate policy flows to the statehouses
articles.description: Almost no one ran on climate change this fall, but the election may reshape climate policy all the same. Democrats won both houses of Congress, a majority of governorships and — as projected by the National Conference of State Legislatures — control of 25 state legislatures by talking about prices: gasoline, diesel, home heating and […]
articles.content: State Rep. Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) steps to the podium in Detroit with Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) after Democrats retook the majority on the Michigan House and retained control of the Senate. Puri is on track to be the next Speaker of the House, while Brinks was elected at lieutenant governor earlier Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Almost no one ran on climate change this fall, but the election may reshape climate policy all the same. Democrats won both houses of Congress, a majority of governorships and — as projected by the National Conference of State Legislatures — control of 25 state legislatures by talking about prices: gasoline, diesel, home heating and above all — electricity. Geoff Garin, a Democratic pollster who works with the advocacy group Climate Power, told Capital & Main that nearly three-quarters of Democratic candidates in battleground-state races ran at least one ad about energy costs. “The old Republican mantras of ‘drill, baby, drill’ and American energy dominance were and are wholly irrelevant to the current energy debate,” Garin said. “Instead, the energy debate now is focused on [President Donald] Trump’s ill-conceived war, on data centers, on price gouging by oil companies and on Trump’s war on clean energy.” Indeed, in a NBC News exit poll, 74% of voters pointed to the war in Iran as a major factor in their vote and 86% said they were concerned about utility costs. In Garin’s polling, 53% said producing more wind and solar power would make energy more affordable — with one in five saying renewables would make it much more affordable. Voters who rank climate first in their priorities, meanwhile, showed up early. Across the 21 states where the nonprofit Environmental Voter Project works, 49.3% of its identified climate voters cast early ballots, said Nathaniel Stinnett, the group’s founder. That was up from 41% in the 2024 presidential election and 32.5% in the 2022 midterms, he told Capital & Main. “Even if politicians weren’t talking about climate, climate voters were sure thinking about politics, because they ran to the polls to vote as soon as possible,” Stinnett said. “I think we can safely say that the climate crisis is already impacting our political choices and behavior in a profound way.” In Washington, the answer over the next two years is oversight and leverage but little new law. In state capitals and town halls, it could be a great deal more. Washington: Subpoenas, spending and one live bill Neither Democratic majority approaches the two-thirds needed to override a veto, and Trump has promised to use his freely. David Victor, a professor of public policy at the University of California, San Diego, predicted a stalemate at the federal level. That leaves three tools. The first is the gavel. Starting in January, Democratic chairs in the House reportedly plan to use subpoena power to investigate budget cuts, staff reductions and pollution-limit reversals at the Environmental Protection Agency under Administrator Lee Zeldin. They also plan to examine deals in which energy companies traded offshore wind leases for fossil fuel development or won exemptions from Clean Air Act requirements. The second is the purse. Democrats intend to use must-pass spending bills — broad budget bills required to finance federal agencies, military operations, national parks and public services — to restore money for climate research, disaster resilience and clean energy grants. They also may try to revive clean energy tax credits repealed in the 2025 reconciliation law, framing them as a way to cut utility bills. A Senate majority can also block nominees to the EPA, the Energy Department and the federal bench. The third is the one major bill that’s actually already moving. The Senate voted 73-25 on Nov. 9 to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, designed to speed reviews of power plants, transmission lines and data centers. Democrats are split. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, voted no, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has voiced his opposition. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), in line to chair the House Committee on Natural Resources, wants amendments that would shield clean energy projects from agency discrimination, end federal buyouts of offshore wind leases and make data centers pay for their own power needs. “Voters sent a clear message last week that they want better deals than the ones they’ve gotten under unified Republican leadership,” said Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), a member of the environment committee who won reelection in the midterms. Democrats, he said, owe voters a deal “that delivers clean energy megawatts and jobs, near- and long-term savings on energy bills, and real climate benefits without leaving so many important members of our community on the losing side of the ledger.” The oil and gas industry has a different take on the election results. Mike Sommers, chief executive of the American Petroleum Institute, said the affordability message was unmistakable and called the permitting bill the place for bipartisan cooperation to start. The White House said Trump remained committed to reliable, affordable and secure energy. However, the incoming class of Democrats is not of one mind. U.S. Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas promised to protect oil and gas jobs. Rep.-elect Cait Conley (D-N.Y.) framed climate change as a “national security crisis” and called for federal investment in solar, wind and geothermal power and a return to the Paris climate agreement. Rep.-elect Will Lawrence, a 36-year-old co-founder of the climate advocacy group Sunrise Movement who won a swing seat in Michigan, campaigned for state and federal moratoriums on hyperscale data centers — and, as Grist reported, has moved away from the Green New Deal’s massive build-out toward the politics of community control over projects and clean energy. The states: Six new trifectas The most immediate changes are expected where Democrats won the governor’s office and both legislative chambers: Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. The party also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. Pennsylvania has the biggest runway. Democrats flipped the state Senate to cement the first trifecta since 1993, and lawmakers plan to pass long-stalled bills streamlining community solar, warehouse solar and battery storage while barring local governments from banning renewable projects. Gov. Josh Shapiro, who has presidential aspirations, has also proposed a carbon cap-and-trade program, which sets a hard cap on emissions, similar to what California and other states have on the books. In Michigan and Minnesota, restored trifectas are likely to protect laws requiring 100% clean electricity by 2040 from repeal and open the door to grid modernization bills. In Arizona and Wisconsin, new majorities could pursue the renewable standards and decarbonization targets that Republican legislatures blocked for years. Utility regulators are shifting too. Democrats won both open seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission for a 3-2 majority, their first majority in decades, and new appointments in Michigan and Arizona are expected to bring tougher scrutiny of utility spending on fossil fuels. Michigan voters went further, approving a measure that bars state-regulated utilities such as DTE Energy from contributing to the campaigns of officials who oversee them. The bill was backed by U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed. A separate measure to replace DTE Energy with a public utility was narrowly defeated. Local: The data center revolt Closer to home, the story was almost entirely data centers. Voters in 10 states decided 41 local measures, 21 of them in Ohio, and 32 with reported results favoring limits. Pataskala and Granville, Ohio, approved bans on facilities above 25 megawatts with 74% and 82% of the vote. Newly elected local officials in states such as in Pennsylvania and Virginia campaigned on the same promise — reining in data centers. They are expected to tighten zoning, require new facilities to procure their own renewable power and keep utilities from passing grid upgrade costs on to residential ratepayers. Not every local measure said no. Voters in Eugene, Oregon, approved a Clean Energy Fund that places a 2% license fee on large retailers such as Amazon and Walmart to pay for renewable energy and job training. It is expected to raise at least $15 million a year by 2030 and was modeled on Portland’s 2018 fund, which has invested $1.7 billion. The local votes set up the next fight. Pennsylvania Democrats want to stop towns from banning solar farms even as towns across the Midwest vote to ban data centers — and legislatures weighing statewide rules will have to decide whether to codify those bans or override them. Garin, the Democratic pollster, said the politics favored his side. Each of those issues, he said, “gave Democrats the high ground in the energy debate, and I think that that will continue to be the case as we move from elections into legislating and policymaking.” Copyright Capital & Main 2026

“Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science
articles.description: Modern genetics does not support claims of innate racial differences in intelligence.
articles.content: At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US). These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements. These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.Read full article Comments

articles.title: California’s reproductive privacy law has its first case: a woman investigated after stillbirth
articles.description: A woman is suing the city of Los Angeles as well as detectives within the Los Angeles Police Department for allegedly unlawful interrogation and investigation following a stillbirth she had in 2024 — two years after California authorized the right for patients to sue for being investigated due to their pregnancy outcomes. This is the […]
articles.content: An anonymous California plaintiff alleges that after she experienced a stillbirth in 2024, police shackled and interrogated her at the hospital and then pursued a homicide investigation, despite being told by a medical examiner that fetal demise had occurred in utero. (Photo by Thomas Barwick/Getty Images).A woman is suing the city of Los Angeles as well as detectives within the Los Angeles Police Department for allegedly unlawful interrogation and investigation following a stillbirth she had in 2024 — two years after California authorized the right for patients to sue for being investigated due to their pregnancy outcomes. This is the first known lawsuit under the state’s Reproductive Privacy Act, which was amended in 2022 to prohibit the state from taking punitive action based on pregnancy decisions and outcomes. California’s strong right-to-sue protections could become a legal roadmap for other states, said Sara Ainsworth, one of the attorneys representing the plaintiff, who was granted anonymity Thursday and is referred to in the complaint as Jane Doe. The plaintiff alleges that in November 2024 she was unhoused, living in a city shelter and menstruating irregularly due to her epilepsy medication. An emergency visit for stomach pains revealed she was pregnant, but the fetus did not have a heartbeat. According to the complaint, Doe was initially informed she was still in the first trimester and could miscarry at home but subsequently learned she was around 29 weeks’ pregnant. She passed significant blood clots in the shelter toilet, left without flushing and was taken by ambulance to the hospital and treated for significant blood loss, the complaint says, also noting that Doe didn’t realize she had passed the stillbirth. According to the complaint, police showed up at the hospital, shackled her to a bed and interrogated her for hours, telling her that a fetus had been found outside the shelter. “This was the first time Ms. Doe learned that she had passed into the toilet. And it was the first time she heard that someone had reportedly moved the fetus from the toilet to an alley outside the shelter,” the complaint said. The complaint alleges police continued to pursue a homicide investigation for about a year despite being told by a medical examiner that fetal demise had occurred in utero. The Los Angeles Police Department declined to comment citing the pending litigation. “All the different things that they did to Ms. Doe are a violation of the Reproductive Privacy Act,” said Ainsworth, chief legal and policy director at pregnancy-rights nonprofit If/When/How, which helped California pass the right-to-sue law and filed the complaint late last week alongside law firm BraunHagey & Borden LLP. “It’s very important to show the state actors in California that they must abide by the law, which prohibits criminalizing somebody,” Ainsworth said. At least 13 states and the District of Columbia have in recent years enacted measures to ensure protections for people’s pregnancy decisions and outcomes, including California, Colorado, Hawaii, Illinois, Michigan, Missouri, Montana, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia and Washington. But among the few other places that explicitly allow damages suits — including D.C., Colorado and Illinois — California is the only state to eliminate common legal immunities for law enforcement, Ainsworth said. More miscarriages criminally investigated three years into post-Dobbs abortion bans Women in other states have sued for facing criminal charges after a pregnancy loss, including Brittany Watts in Ohio, who last year sued the city of Warren, city policy officers and a hospital after she was arrested and charged with abuse of a corpse following a miscarriage in her home. But Ainsworth noted that in other states it can be harder to determine who’s accountable. “It is typically hard, unfortunately, to hold government officials accountable for wrongful criminalization because of legal barriers,” she said. “The Reproductive Privacy Act in California explicitly not only allows a private right of action but eliminates some of those immunities, allowing government actors who normally are shielded to actually be held accountable for their actions.” In the first three years after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, more than 900 women faced criminal charges for conduct related to their pregnancies. The vast majority of the charges were for child abuse, neglect or endangerment, most related to substance use during pregnancy. But some involved allegations related to failing to obtain prenatal care or other actions taken or not taken during pregnancy or after pregnancy loss. In California, Doe alleges she had to leave the shelter after police told reporters they suspected a homicide and headlines circulated about a newborn baby dropped from a fourth-floor window. In February 2025, she contacted a legal helpline run by If/When/How, and started working with litigation counsel Shantal McNeil, who helped Doe navigate the investigation and petitioned the city attorney not to bring charges. McNeil said reputational damage and other harms often outlast these types of arrests and investigations, even when charges are dropped or never filed. She said police often investigate vulnerable women like the California plaintiff, who according to her attorneys, is a young woman. “People mistakenly think that every pregnancy ends in a healthy baby, or that if this circumstance would happen to them, they would respond differently. … So, if you don’t act in the way that (police) think you should, it’s suddenly suspicious or criminal behavior,” McNeil said. “To us, this is what the hospital told her, ‘Go home, you’re having a miscarriage.’ So the fact that any of this happened because of that or after that is quite mind boggling.” Stateline reporter Sofia Resnick can be reached at sresnick@stateline.org. SERVICE CIRCUIT: Richmond Rotary Club lives motto and mission
articles.content: Michigan’s Richmond Rotary Club recently held a successful fundraiser for three of its many good causes, living up to its motto: Service Above Self. A Rotary club brings together local business and professional leaders and other civic-minded people for community and humanitarian service. Game on Cancer is a charity through Henry Ford Health that helps cancer patients with housing, food, utility bills, transportation to appointments, and conducting research on therapies to treat cancer. For more than a decade, the program has helped over 12,000 patients and their families with donations of about $9.7 million. Great Lakes Burn Camp is located along Pretty Lake near Kalamazoo. It is 287 wooded acres where children who have burn injuries can go — for free — to swim, practice archery, go boating and waterskiing, use the high ropes, and sit around campfires. There are the usual arts and crafts projects, cookouts, as well as outdoor movie night, a dance and fireworks. There is a winter camp also. There are 15,000 children who are hospitalized with burn injuries each year in the U.S. The camp is billed as a place where such children can “laugh, play, heal and grow with others.” A Fisher House is described as a home away from home for family when a veteran is hospitalized in a Department of Veterans Affairs medical facility. There are Fisher Houses operated by Fisher House Michigan in Ann Arbor and in Detroit near the hospitals. Fisher Houses have saved veterans’ families nearly $700 million for lodging and transportation. By supporting it with about $50,000, Rotarians say they are “serving those who served.” The Rotary club meets at 12:15 p.m. Tuesdays at Hamlin Pub, 66771 Gratiot Ave., Richmond. Rick Landuyt is president-elect of the club. Another club cause that is close to his heart is The Salvation Army. “I’ve been trying to kickstart bellringing for the Salvation Army,” Landuyt said. “They came and spoke to us. Now every year we have four locations, and people work one- or two-hour shifts from the day after Thanksgiving to Christmas Eve. It’s perfect for kids. I had a couple of kids come up and they sang for half an hour. But I’m having a hard time getting bell ringers right now.” Rotarians were featured in a newspaper story last year. “That helped us get close to 800 bellringers. We’re starting to take out the kettles this week,” he said. Landuyt can be reached at 313-407-9654. As a cancer survivor himself, Landuyt was drawn to the Game On Cancer project. “It helps people not have to choose between electricity and food, or chemo. With Burn Camp, a member of our club brought it to our attention and I was like, this is like out of a movie, a kid is burned, and is made fun of at school because kids can be mean. And then they go to this camp apprehensive but they end up making lifetime friends. It’s a memory that they’ve got for the rest of their life, and we want to keep giving them that,” he said. “We don’t ever care if our name is on a plaque or not. That’s not our purpose. It’s all about does our money do good? Having the Rotary club is like having a kid and watching them grow and become better than you are,” he said. He credited Carol Walters, the first woman Rotarian in the club, for spreading the word about Rotary among local schools. A Peace Pole is a structure that says “May peace prevail on earth” in several languages. “A couple of years ago we put up a Peace Pole,” Landuyt said. “One of the student groups at Richmond High School thought that would be a great idea. There are several benches around it, right outside one of the entrances where they can sit around and just talk or just sit and look at the different languages that say peace to all. It’s by the entrances so it gets a lot of traffic. What we’re always doing is planning what we could help with, how to promote our causes, and our charities.” He said they welcome more people in business and the community who would like to network with others in Rotary. The club often gives donations to nonprofits when their representatives come to meetings and inform Rotarians on what they do for the community. “We’ve heard about a lot of different things. We’re just looking to give back,” he said. “People from Meals on Wheels came and spoke and a couple of people from our organization opted into that. We pass along information we learn from them and we can also opt to join in a little bit if it touches us. Interest in these causes starts with one person and it grows into a little bit of a fever, then camaraderie, and we have enthusiasm. We can show people without telling them; they can see what it’s doing for us and others and they say ‘I want to be part of that’.” People in the greater Richmond area can support the Rotary club by buying gourmet nuts and candy on display at local banks and other neighborhood businesses. Its big red food trailer has an annual presence at the Armada Fair. The downtown Mount Clemens Santa Parade starts at 10 a.m. Saturday, Nov. 21. Veterans and service clubs participating include presenting sponsor the Mount Clemens Lions Club, AMVETS Post 29 honor guard, AMVETS Post 29 Riders, silver sponsor Mount Clemens Goodfellows, The Freemasons, the Tomcat Squadron and Training Ship Tomcat of the U.S. Naval Sea Cadet Corps, Fraternal Order of Eagles Mount Clemens, bronze sponsor Kiwanis Club of Mount Clemens, and the Mount Clemens Rotary Club. The parade route runs through downtown Mount Clemens on Main Street from Church Street to Clinton Street. Santa Claus arrives at the end of the parade. Gov. Gretchen Whitmer fund has raised $40 million from secret donors
articles.content: LANSING — A nonprofit organization that supports Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer collected more than $3 million in 2025 from contributors whose names didn't have to be disclosed to the public, according to a new tax filing. The group, Road to Michigan's Future, launched in January 2020 and has now reported raising a total of more than $40 million while Whitmer has held the state's top office and had the power to sign or veto bills from the Legislature. The organization has bankrolled efforts to promote the Democrat's policy proposals and has frequently compensated key members of her political team. While many officeholders in Lansing have set up nonprofit groups to raise money from secret contributors and to advance their political goals, the Whitmer team's level of secret fundraising has outpaced everyone else. The donors' names don't have to be reported because the groups aren't expressly being used to seek people's votes and they fall outside traditional campaign finance laws. Plus, legislators have refused to set up other disclosure standards to cover their own nonprofits. In an interview, state Rep. Tom Kunse, R-Clare, an open government advocate, labeled the undisclosed money flowing into the governor-tied Road to Michigan's Future disappointing. "Democracy dies in darkness," Kunse said. "Transparency is so important in the political world.” Republican former Gov. Rick Snyder's similar nonprofit NERD Fund raised about $2.2 million overall while it was operational from 2011 through 2013. Mark Fisk, a Democratic political consultant and the spokesman for Road to Michigan's Future, has previously said the group follows "all IRS rules and requirements to the letter of the law." “At Road to Michigan’s Future, we are proud of our continued mission to support Gov. Whitmer’s agenda of lowering costs, putting money back into Michiganders’ pockets and promoting affordability for Michigan families," Fisk said in a statement on Nov. 20. The group's website says it's "proud to keep our state headed in the right direction under the leadership of Gov. Gretchen Whitmer." The new tax document, submitted to the IRS, was dated Monday, Nov. 16, and covered the 2025 calendar year. The $3 million raised represented the lowest fundraising total Road to Michigan's Future has posted in an individual year. It came in Whitmer's second-to-last year in the governor's office. Because of term limits, she couldn't run for reelection in 2026. The group's biggest fundraising year was in 2022 — Whitmer's reelection year — when it raised $12.9 million. Three individual donors gave a third of the money Road to Michigan's Future collected in 2025. One undisclosed donor gave $550,000 to the governor's fund, another gave $250,000, and a third gave $200,000, according to the tax filing, which didn't have to include the contributors' names. Unless the donors have to report their giving in other filings, it will be difficult for the public to know what interests they might have had in policy matters before the governor. Road to Michigan's Future reported spending $3.4 million in 2025 and having $4.6 million available at the end of the year. Of its 2025 expenses, $1.2 million went to salaries and wages: Heather Ricketts, who was Whitmer's campaign compliance director, was paid $223,500; and Brieann Sauer, who was her campaign's finance director, was paid $155,000, according to the tax document. Road to Michigan's Future reported $70,798 in office expenses and $581,253 in spending on conferences, conventions and meetings in 2025. It gave $119,200 to a Michigan Democratic Party account and $10,000 to the Yeshiva Beth Yehudah Foundation in 2025.

articles.title: Israeli settlers' move into a Palestinian neighborhood brings deadly violence to Jericho's doorstep
articles.description: Israeli settlers' move into a Palestinian neighborhood brings deadly violence to Jericho's doorstep AP News Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say The Guardian Far-right MKs back new Jericho settlement in an effort to repeal Oslo Accords The Jerusalem Post Two Israeli teens wounded in terror car-ramming, ax attack near West Bank settlement Ynetnews Israeli military says it will no
articles.content: JERICHO, West Bank (AP) — For years, this lush Palestinian city was an oasis of calm in the occupied West Bank. Jericho’s warm weather drew tourists year-round and its perch low in the Jordan Valley kept it somewhat isolated from the violence elsewhere in the territory. But that relative peace was shattered this week when Palestinians said Israeli settlers who had newly infiltrated the outskirts of Jericho shot and killed a 72-year-old woman during clashes with local youth. The killing late Monday of Fadda Fheidat came just days after the settlers had seized a cluster of Palestinian homes they said they purchased — a claim that rights groups and Palestinian residents contest. The takeover was the first time in decades that Israelis had settled within a residential neighborhood around a major Palestinian city. And now, as armed settlers patrol their streets, Palestinian residents say the violence has raised fears that a new phase of settlement expansion is reaching West Bank cities once considered safe from encroaching settlers. Israel has occupied the West Bank since it captured the territory, along with east Jerusalem and the Gaza Strip, from Jordan and Egypt in the 1967 Mideast war. Since then, it has built a network of settlements for more than half a million Israelis on land Palestinians seek for a future independent state. The international community overwhelmingly considers the settlements illegal. But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing government has approved more than 100 new settlements during its tenure. Settlers have also erected unauthorized outposts, which they’ve used to attack Palestinian shepherds, rampage through communities and drive people from their homes. The seizure of the homes in al-Duyuk al-Tahta followed a similar pattern, residents and rights groups say, starting with the construction of a new outpost nearby in 2024. The neighborhood lies just outside Jericho’s city limits, near a prized archaeological site that Israel has invested in developing as a tourist destination. “We are writing a new chapter of Jewish life. We have returned home,” Israel Ganz, who heads the local council governing Israeli settlements in the area, declared on social media after the settlers moved in on Nov. 4. The Israeli rights group B’Tselem described the settlers’ arrival as the latest in a series of increasingly bold and largely unchallenged efforts to drive Palestinians from their land. It warned of “a reality similar to Hebron ” — the only city where Israeli settlers have for decades lived under military protection in the heart of a built-up Palestinian urban area. The settlers’ arrival introduces a permanent Israeli presence “with increased military deployment, restrictions on Palestinian movement, and settler militia violence and intimidation, which will affect the lives of tens of thousands of Palestinians,” the group said in a statement. A major turning point came in February when settlers from the nearby outpost, emboldened by Israeli demolition orders for several houses on the edge of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, drove trucks and tractors into the community and spent nearly eight hours ransacking and bulldozing homes, Palestinian residents said. Soon after that, the Israeli government legalized the outpost. By October, settlers had taken some of the Palestinian community’s farmland and began setting up new irrigation systems. On Nov. 4, dozens of Israelis, some of them armed, moved into eight Palestinian homes. The settlers say they have proof-of-purchase documents for the houses, but Palestinian residents say they don’t know how, when or by whom the properties were sold. Palestinian officials and Israeli human rights groups have questioned the legality of the sales under both Israeli and Palestinian laws. Most of the properties sit on farmland that Palestinian shepherds have grazed for generations and that Israel classifies as state land. Under Israeli law, plots designated as state land generally cannot be privately bought or sold. Under the Palestinian Authority, the internationally backed body that administers semiautonomous parts of the West Bank, including Jericho, selling land to Israelis is a criminal offense. Almost immediately after the settlers moved in, they began policing the neighborhood, often with guns and in ATVs, Palestinian residents said. “They started to control our lives,” said Mustapha Fheidat, a farmer whose extended family makes up much of the population in al-Duyuk al-Tahta. “They stop us and ask for our IDs and what we’re doing here. They prevent us getting from the main road to our farms.” According to four members of the Fheidat family, it was one of these settler patrols that set off Monday’s deadly clash, after settlers hurled insults at Palestinian residents, who responded by pelting them with rocks. Israel’s military said in a statement that the sequence of events that led to Monday’s shooting death were under investigation. Citing testimony collected by soldiers at the scene, it said the clash erupted after a Palestinian driver ”carried out an attack by ramming” into an Israeli settler’s vehicle as youths threw rocks at the settlers. Fadda Fheidat was “likely injured by fire from an Israeli civilian,” the military said. No arrests of Israelis were announced in connection with the shooting. Two Palestinian men were arrested in connection with the “ramming” incident, the military said. Members of the Fheidat family who witnessed the violence denied the collision was intentional, saying it happened when Fadda Fheidat’s son was rushing to the scene of his mother’s shooting and skidded into the settler’s vehicle. They said Fadda Fheidat and her daughter-in-law, Na’ima, were driving a relative who had been shot to a nearby hospital but turned back after Palestinians warned that more settlers were on the road ahead. The violence was still underway when the women returned home. As they got out of the car, Na’ima Fheidat said she heard her children scream: “‘Grandma has been killed! Grandma has been killed!’” Ahmed Fheidat was inside his home when he heard the shouting and gunfire. He rushed outside and found his sister-in-law lying on the ground with a gunshot to the head. “Her skull was completely broken. My hand was full of blood,” he said. He carried her inside to wait for an ambulance, barely noticing that he, too, had been shot in the leg.
